applyTo: "**/*.dwl,**/src/main/mule/**/*.xml,**/src/test/munit/**/*.xml"
description: "DataWeave rules. Read before reading or changing any DataWeave: a .dwl file, or a Transform Message script or inline expression in Mule or MUnit XML."

# DataWeave changes

Follow the project's existing DataWeave conventions first. Use documentation for the project's DataWeave version; links below are 2.9 (Mule 4.9) examples. Items marked (documented) are stated in MuleSoft documentation. Items marked (CLI) were observed by running the DataWeave CLI (runtime 2.12.2, at its default and at language levels 2.4–2.9), not taken from documentation; confirm them on the project's runtime when they decide the outcome.

Three reference files hold situational detail. Read the one that applies before writing that code:

- [Operator and function behavior](../skills/team-mule-guardrails/references/dataweave-operators.md): before using `-` or `--`, range selectors, `take`/`drop`/`slice`, `update`, `mask` or the `dw::util::Tree` helpers, or `isBlank`/`trim`/`upper`, or writing a recursive function.
- [Output formats](../skills/team-mule-guardrails/references/dataweave-output-formats.md): before changing an `output` directive or its writer properties, or writing CSV or XML.
- [Performance and large payloads](../skills/team-mule-guardrails/references/dataweave-performance.md): before optimizing a script, reading large inputs, or changing lookups or streaming.

## DataWeave inside Mule XML

Most scripts in a Mule project sit in the flow file, in a Transform Message or an inline `#[...]` expression. Leave each script where the project keeps it: do not move an inline script to a `.dwl` file, or back, unless that is the task.

- A Transform Message holds one script per output: `ee:set-payload` and `ee:set-attributes` under `ee:message`, and `ee:set-variable` under `ee:variables`. Each is either inline in `<![CDATA[ ... ]]>` or an external file named by `resource`, which is resolved statically and cannot use `${...}` placeholders. Change only the output the task concerns. See [Transform Message XML](https://docs.mulesoft.com/mule-runtime/4.9/transform-dataweave-xml-reference).
- Inside CDATA, write DataWeave unescaped: `<`, `&` and quotes are literal there, and XML entities such as `&lt;` are not decoded. The one sequence that cannot appear is `]]>`, which ends the section; valid DataWeave can contain it (`arr[idx[0]]>5`, CLI), so put a space before the `>`.
- In an attribute such as `value="#[...]"`, the expression is XML attribute text: write `<` as `&lt;` and `&` as `&amp;`, and inside a double-quoted attribute use single-quoted DataWeave strings (CLI) or `&quot;`. Keep the escaping style the file already uses. After any edit the file must still be well-formed XML; a script that is valid DataWeave can still break it. See [XML character data](https://www.w3.org/TR/xml/#syntax) and [CDATA sections](https://www.w3.org/TR/xml/#sec-cdata-sect).
- An inline expression has no header unless it is written on one line with `---`, for example `#[output application/json --- payload]`. With no `output` directive the format follows the inputs: `application/java` when there is no input, the shared MIME type when all inputs agree, and an error when they differ (documented). Do not assume JSON; keep or add the directive where the consumer needs a specific format. See [DataWeave header](https://docs.mulesoft.com/dataweave/2.9/dataweave-language-introduction#dw_header).
- Keep `%dw 2.0`, the `output` directive and its writer properties when changing a script body, unless the task is to change the output.
- Scripts in a flow use Mule's predefined variables (`payload`, `attributes`, `vars`, `error`, `correlationId` and others) and Mule functions such as `p()`. The standalone DataWeave CLI has none of them: `vars`, `attributes` and `p` failed as unresolved references (CLI). To test a script outside Mule, copy it to a scratch file outside the project and supply those values as inputs, or cover the flow with MUnit. See [predefined variables](https://docs.mulesoft.com/dataweave/2.9/dataweave-variables-context) and [Mule functions](https://docs.mulesoft.com/dataweave/2.9/dw-mule).

## Correctness

- Check the executing runtime and the app's `minMuleVersion`, which sets the language level (Mule 4.4 gives 2.4, through 4.9 giving 2.9); `%dw 2.0` alone does not identify the engine version, and some behaviors below differ by level. See [versioning behavior](https://docs.mulesoft.com/dataweave/2.9/dataweave-versioning-behavior). State input/output MIME types and the relevant shape. Define behavior for absent, null, empty, malformed, and unexpected-type values before writing the mapping.
- Use `default` only when the contract intentionally treats missing or null values alike; it does not replace `false`, `0`, empty strings, arrays or objects. `isEmpty` is true for `null`, `""`, `[]` and `{}`. When absent and explicit null differ, check key presence (`payload.field?` is true for an explicit null) separately from the value. Do not silently convert malformed amounts or dates into valid-looking defaults. `("abc" as Number) default 0` returned `0` at levels 2.4–2.9 in the native CLI, but this is not portable exception handling: MuleSoft documents `com.mulesoft.dw.defaultOperator.disableExceptionHandling=true` from level 2.5, which disables catching runtime exceptions. Validate malformed input explicitly and verify recovery behavior on the actual runtime and compatibility settings. See [system properties](https://docs.mulesoft.com/dataweave/2.9/dataweave-system-properties) and [DataWeave defaults](https://docs.mulesoft.com/dataweave/2.9/dataweave-cookbook-defaults).
- Every `if` needs an `else`, and every branch or `match` case should return a value the output contract allows, not an accidental `null`.
- Compare with `==` unless the contract allows cross-type equality; `~=` coerces (`1 ~= "1"` is true). `not` negates everything after it while `!` negates only the next operand (`not true or true` is false). Infix function calls such as `mod`, `map` and `matches` bind more loosely than comparisons and arithmetic: `i mod 3 == 0` passes `3 == 0` to `mod` (CLI). Add parentheses. See [operators](https://docs.mulesoft.com/dataweave/2.9/dw-operators) and [precedence](https://docs.mulesoft.com/dataweave/2.9/dataweave-flow-control-precedence).
- Overloaded functions resolve to the first declaration that accepts the arguments, so declare specific types before `Any`. See [functions](https://docs.mulesoft.com/dataweave/2.9/dataweave-functions).
- Give `reduce` an initial accumulator (`(item, acc = 0) -> ...`); otherwise the first element becomes the accumulator, which can change the result type, and an empty array returns `null`. See [reduce](https://docs.mulesoft.com/dataweave/2.9/dw-core-functions-reduce).
- `readUrl` on a network URL makes a real call that processor mocks do not intercept; use `classpath://` resources in tests or isolate the call.
- Preserve required order and duplicates. Do not apply sorting, deduplication, trimming, or case conversion unless the contract calls for them.
- Check realistic samples and adversarial boundaries: zero/false, absent/null, empty arrays/strings, malformed numbers/dates, and Unicode when relevant. Test the transform directly or through MUnit using sanitized fixtures; successful JSON parsing alone does not test DataWeave. If the project already uses the DataWeave testing framework (`src/test/dw`), add tests there; do not add that dependency without approval.

### Numbers and money

- Preserve exact decimal values through parsing, arithmetic, Java/connector boundaries and comparison; a binary floating-point round trip can lose money precision.
- `as Number` is more lenient than most contracts (CLI): it accepts `.5`, `5.`, `+5`, `0012` and exponents (`"1e3"` becomes `1E+3`), and rejects surrounding spaces, `1,000` and `NaN`. When the contract defines the allowed format of numeric strings, check the string against it before coercing.
- Scale is not kept: `1.10` becomes `1.1` after arithmetic, `as String`, and in CSV or XML output; only an unchanged input number passes through JSON as written (CLI). Trailing zeros are stripped from language level 2.5 (Mule 4.5); at 2.4 the literal `1.10` stayed `1.10` (CLI; documented as `com.mulesoft.dw.stripTrailingZeroes`), so a `minMuleVersion` upgrade can change output. Format explicitly when output needs fixed decimals (`as String {format: "0.00"}`).
- Formatting rounds half up (`2.345` gives `"2.35"`, `2.5` gives `"3"`) and `round(-2.5)` is `-3` (CLI). If the contract requires another rounding mode, pass `roundMode`: `2.5 as String {format: "0", roundMode: "HALF_EVEN"}` and `toString(2.5, "0", null, "HALF_EVEN")` from `dw::util::Coercions` both give `"2"` (CLI). See [toString](https://docs.mulesoft.com/dataweave/2.9/dw-coercions-functions-tostring). Division keeps 34 significant digits, so `(10 / 3) * 3` is not `10`; multiply before dividing and round once at the end. `avg([])` and division by zero fail (CLI).
- Avoid locale-dependent formats unless the contract names a locale (`locale: "de"` writes `1.234,50`).

### Dates and times

- With a `format`, the default parsing mode silently turns `02/30/2026` into `02/28/2026` (CLI). If invalid dates must fail, use `mode: "STRICT"` with `uuuu` for the year; `STRICT` with `yyyy` rejected valid dates (CLI). Never use `YYYY` for a calendar year: it is the week-based year (`2026-12-29` formats as `2027-12-29`, CLI). See [type coercion](https://docs.mulesoft.com/dataweave/2.9/dataweave-types-coercion).
- Say whether a value is an instant or a local time, and in which zone. A string without an offset coerced `as DateTime` became UTC whatever the machine's time zone (CLI); parse it as `LocalDateTime` and attach the zone the contract defines. Date-times with different offsets compare by instant (CLI). Adding `|P1M|` to January 31 gives February 28. In `America/Chicago`, a time in the spring-forward gap moved forward an hour and a repeated autumn time took the earlier, daylight offset (CLI); state how gaps and repeated hours are handled when local times matter.

### Nulls, strings and objects

- `"a" ++ null` fails at runtime, while `map`, `filter`, `joinBy` and `sizeOf` on `null` return `null` rather than an empty result (CLI). Default optional parts before concatenating, and decide whether a null collection means an empty one.
- `splitBy` drops trailing empty fields (`"a,b,"` gives `["a","b"]`) and returns `[""]` for `""` (CLI). Use the CSV reader for delimited records where empty fields matter.
- `++` on objects with a shared key keeps both keys: JSON output repeats the key and `.key` returns the first value (CLI). Use `mergeWith` from `dw::core::Objects` (right-hand values win) or remove the key first. JSON input with duplicate keys also keeps both.
- Conditional array items and object fields need parentheses: `[(x) if cond]`, `{(key: v) if cond}`; without them the script does not compile (CLI). Use `flatMap` instead of `flatten` around a `map`.
- Whole-object equality is key-order sensitive: `{a: 1, b: 2} == {b: 2, a: 1}` is false, and `distinctBy $` and `contains` also treat reordered objects as different (CLI). Compare or deduplicate by the relevant fields.

### Selectors, lookups and ordering

- On objects, `payload.key` returns only the first matching key; use `.*key` when duplicates must all be read, and `..*key` for every nested match including duplicate keys. On XML input, single-value selection can depend on sibling shape and compatibility settings: a simple repeated `<name>` returned the first value, but mapping across differently shaped `<user>` elements returned the second name for one user (CLI). Use `.*key` and choose explicitly when elements can repeat; do not rely on a universal first/second outcome from `.key`. See `com.mulesoft.dw.valueSelector.selectsAlwaysFirst` in the [system properties](https://docs.mulesoft.com/dataweave/2.9/dataweave-system-properties). A lookup such as `filter(...)[0]` returns `null` when nothing matches; decide and test what the output should be. Null handling differs between functions (for example `upper(null)` is `null`, `contains(null, x)` is `false`). See [selectors](https://docs.mulesoft.com/dataweave/2.9/dataweave-selectors).
- Object keys are DataWeave `Key` values with a local name, namespace and attributes. Use `key as String` when intentionally comparing only the local name; a key is not equal to a String under `==` (CLI). See [Object type](https://docs.mulesoft.com/dataweave/2.9/dataweave-types#dw_type_object). Indexing an object with a Number selects by position: after `groupBy $.id`, `grouped[201]` returned `null` and `grouped[1]` returned the second group, not key `"1"` (CLI). Convert numeric lookup IDs with `as String`, and wrap computed keys in parentheses (`obj[("k" ++ id)]`).
- `join`, `leftJoin` and `outerJoin` from `dw::core::Arrays` return `{l, r}` pairs in the left list's order, one per match, so a left item with two matches appears twice. An unmatched item has no `r` (or `l`) key at all, so test with `pair.r?`. Keys are compared as strings: numeric `1` matched string `"1"` (CLI).
- `orderBy` keeps ties in input order and compares strings by code point (`"A"`, `"B"`, `"a"`, `"b"`; `"10"` before `"9"`). It failed on `null` sort keys. At language levels 2.4–2.9 it coerced mixed strings and numbers with only a warning (`[5, 1, "10"]` gave `[1, "10", 5]`), while the native CLI's default level rejected them (CLI). This does not establish every later Mule engine's behavior; see `com.mulesoft.dw.stableOrderBy` in the version's [system properties](https://docs.mulesoft.com/dataweave/2.9/dataweave-system-properties). Convert sort keys to one type and handle nulls first.

## Performance

No construct is universally faster. Ask for or state the expected payload size, then change performance only with a reason you can measure on the target runtime. CLI timings come from a native binary, not Mule's JVM; use them for relative scale only. Read the [performance reference](../skills/team-mule-guardrails/references/dataweave-performance.md) before changing a script for speed or memory.

- `deferred=true` streams output to the next processor, but errors raised while writing are not handled by the Transform, and an HTTP client may already have received status 200 and gets a truncated body; use it only when the flow and its callers can tolerate that.
- Avoid `output application/dw` in production processing; it was about three times slower than JSON (CLI). Preserve deliberate test resources that use this [debugging/testing format](https://docs.mulesoft.com/dataweave/2.9/dataweave-formats-dw). Remove `log()` calls before merging: they print in that format, logging each of 20,000 records made the script about 20 times slower, and they can expose payload data in logs.
- Do not change DataWeave memory system properties (`com.mulesoft.dw.*`) without measurements; they affect the whole runtime. See [memory management](https://docs.mulesoft.com/dataweave/2.9/dataweave-memory-management).

## Maintainability

- Prefer readable transformations with small named functions or variables when they remove meaningful duplication. Put functions reused across scripts in a module under `src/main/resources` (for example `modules/`, imported as `modules::Name`) following the project's layout. Do not introduce a folder named `dw`: it shares the `dw::` prefix with the built-in modules. Logic shared across applications belongs in a DataWeave library published to Exchange and added as a pinned dependency, not copied. See [custom modules](https://docs.mulesoft.com/dataweave/2.9/dataweave-create-module).
- Declare `input`/`output` directives with MIME types where the format matters. Type annotations on variables, parameters and return values, and named types for contract shapes, surface mismatches earlier; they do not replace the null and malformed-value checks above.
